sources.name: Sea Ice Index, Version 4 (G02135)
sources.publisher: NOAA@NSIDC (National Snow and Ice Data Center, CIRES, University of Colorado Boulder)
sources.measures: Arctic and Antarctic sea ice extent (area with at least 15% ice concentration) and sea ice area, in million km2. Daily values plus monthly files, with a 1981-2010 daily climatology.

sources.license: US-government-funded data in the public domain. NSIDC's data-use page (https://nsidc.org/about/data-use-and-copyright) lets you download and use its imagery and text unless a page states otherwise. It asks for a full data citation and forbids reselling photos or imagery. NSIDC/NASA say these data are shared openly without restriction. No formal licence document.
sources.citation: Fetterer, F., Knowles, K., Meier, W. N., Savoie, M., Windnagel, A. K. & Stafford, T. (2025). Sea Ice Index. (G02135, Version 4). [Data Set]. Boulder, Colorado USA. National Snow and Ice Data Center. https://doi.org/10.7265/a98x-0f50. [Date Accessed].
sources.status: Active but at risk. The landing page says the dataset was recently downgraded to a Basic Level of Service because of funding limits. A NOAA@NSIDC notice of 5 May 2025 (NOAA decommissioning) says Basic products stay online but may not be actively maintained, updated or fully supported. The DMSP SSMIS input was lost or degraded in 2025, so v4 switched to JAXA AMSR2. The FY2027 President's budget again proposes deep NOAA cuts.
sources.url_check: Fetched the landing page: DOI and citation present, plus a Basic Level of Service notice. Fetched the v4 release announcement (31 Jul 2025) and the NOAA@NSIDC data-updates page (5 May 2025 service notice; 23 Jul 2025 AMSR2 note). Directory listings for north/monthly/data (12 files, 02-Oct-2026) and north/daily/data. Pulled N_09_extent_v4.0.csv with curl. Header: 'year, mo,source_dataset, region, extent, area'. 1979 row is 7.05; 2024 is 4.35 (NSIDC-0051); 2025 is 4.75 and 2026 is 4.81 (both NSIDC-0803); the 1981-2010 mean is 6.413 (n=30). In the daily CSV the 2026 minimum is 4.574 on 2026-09-12. NSIDC's analysis of 23 Sep 2026 gives 4.60 M km2 on 12 Sep (5-day average), tied for 10th lowest. In S_09_extent_v4.0.csv, 2026 is 17.32 and the lowest year is 2023 at 16.89.
sources.site_use: Main Arctic and Antarctic sea ice charts: a daily spaghetti plot against the 1981-2010 climatology, and September-minimum and March-maximum bar charts. Feeds the Arctic headline. Use the monthly CSVs for the downloadable 'numbers shown'.
sources.caveats: Values from 2025 onward come from AMSR2 (NSIDC-0803). NSIDC says AMSR2 puts the ice edge slightly inboard, so extents are a little smaller. Mark the 2025 change on charts. NSIDC press numbers use a 5-day trailing mean (4.60) while the daily CSV gives 4.574, so label which one is shown. Monthly extent is not the mean of the daily values. Do not splice with OSI SAF (different algorithm).

headline_numbers.statement: Greenland's ice sheet lost 6,196 billion tonnes of ice from 1972 to 2023, and Antarctica's lost 4,779 billion tonnes from 1979 to 2023. Together that added about 30 mm to global sea level.

headline_numbers.statement: How high the seas rise this century depends on our emissions. The likely rise by 2100 is 0.28-0.55 m under very low emissions (SSP1-1.9) versus 0.63-1.01 m under very high emissions (SSP5-8.5).

drilldown_paths: Why is the sea rising? (cause to consequence). GMSL since 1993 (AVISO + NASA-SSH lines) leads to a 'what's adding water' budget: thermal expansion (NCEI thermosteric/OHC), Greenland and Antarctica (IMBIE mm files, with GRACE-FO monthly extension), glaciers (WGMS mmsle by region), and land water (Frederikse JPL_RECON 1900-2018 for the long view). This links to the ocean-heat page and to the atmosphere/emissions domain (the heat comes from the greenhouse effect). It ends at the AR6 scenario slider (low vs high emissions in 2100).

My coastline. Global map of PSMSL tide gauges leads to the station's relative sea level since the 1800s (anomaly against its own 1900-1920 mean), then to why local differs from global (subsidence/uplift; NOAA CO-OPS trend with CI for US stations), then to AR6 regional projections at the nearest location (Zenodo regional files, preprocessed), then to local adaptation resources.

Heat in the ocean. Ocean heat content 0-700 m (1955-) and 0-2000 m (2005-) (NCEI, with IAP cross-check) leads to daily global SST (OISST v2.1), then to the % of ocean in a marine heatwave (computed from the CRW MHW category NetCDF with the area-weighting code published; Copernicus/Mercator bulletin as a labelled external comparison), then to coral heat stress by reef region (CRW virtual-station DHW series) and the 84.4% global bleaching statistic.

Ocean acidification. Atmospheric CO2 at Mauna Loa (atmosphere domain) set beside seawater pCO2 and pH at Station ALOHA, Hawaii (HOT pHcalc_insitu, pCO2calc_insitu). Then global surface pH 1985-2024 (CMEMS OMI), then aragonite saturation at ALOHA (HOT aragsatcalc_insitu) as the impact on shells and coral skeletons.

Ice, pole to pole. Arctic sea ice daily and September minimum (NSIDC G02135) leads to regional seas (OSI SAF v3 regional files, Barents, Kara, etc.) and Antarctic sea ice (NSIDC S files; record lows 2023). Then land ice vs sea ice (only land ice raises sea level), then ice sheets (IMBIE cumulative Gt, SMB vs dynamics), then glaciers by mountain region and single glaciers (WGMS AMCE region/glacier CSVs; GlaMBIE cross-check), ending with mm of sea level per source.

Frozen ground and snow. NH snow cover by month (Rutgers/NOAA CDR, honest that the spring/June loss is large and autumn change is small) leads to permafrost temperature at boreholes (GTN-P API, site charts on a map), then to the consequence: thawing permafrost releases carbon, linking to the emissions domain (feedback loop).
research.action_links:
The causal lever comes straight from the data. AR6 projections show 2100 sea level of 0.28-0.55 m under very low emissions versus 0.63-1.01 m under very high emissions (IPCC AR6 WGI SPM B.5.3; Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.6382554). Every ocean, ice and acidification chart should therefore link to the emissions/energy domain pages ('what drives this') and to the AR6 scenario slider ('what our choices change').

Individuals: cutting personal and household emissions is the upstream fix, via links to the emissions domain. For divers and reef users, NOAA Coral Reef Watch's global bleaching page takes bleaching observation reports (https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/satellite/research/coral_bleaching_report.php). In May 2026 NOAA launched a first-ever standard operating procedure for bleaching monitoring (CRW home page notice, 26 May 2026), so citizen observations feed the official record.

Communities and coastal planners: use the PSMSL station history plus the NASA/IPCC AR6 regional projection for the nearest gauge (https://sealevel.nasa.gov/ipcc-ar6-sea-level-projection-tool). In the US, use the NOAA CO-OPS trend with its confidence interval (moving to the 'Sea Level Trends and Extremes - BETA' site after 30 Sep 2026) to set local planning horizons.

Policymakers: the 'gaps_and_risks' items are actionable on their own terms. Several records used here depend on continued public funding: NSIDC Sea Ice Index (Basic service since 2025), GRACE-FO and its successor GRACE-C (~2028), HOT (NSF), NOAA CRW and NCEI. The site can show a neutral 'data at risk' badge with evidence links, such as the NSIDC Basic-service notice and the CO-OPS retirement banner, so readers can see why sustained observation matters. The site never asks for money and never sells anything.
research.gaps_and_risks:
1) US federal fragility (verified evidence):
- NSIDC G02135 was cut to 'Basic' service (NOAA@NSIDC notice of 5 May 2025). Its SSMIS inputs were lost, so it now depends on JAXA AMSR2.
- NOAA CO-OPS Sea Level Trends carries a banner saying it will be retired after 30 Sep 2026, replaced by a BETA site.
- EPA's Climate Change Indicators section (sea level, ocean heat, snow and ice) was removed in Dec 2025 (E&E News, Washington Post, EDGI). Never link to EPA indicator pages; use upstream producers.
- NOAA STAR LSA GMSL CSVs stop at Feb 2025 (2025.127).
- GRACE-FO is past its prime mission (eoHandbook end-of-life Sep 2026; Senior Review 2026), and GRACE-C is not due until about 2028.
- NCEI reports degraded services during its cloud migration.
- The FY2027 President's budget again proposes eliminating NOAA OAR and cutting NASA science by about 42%. Congress reversed similar FY2026 cuts (H.R. 6938, Jan 2026), but OMB has reportedly been slow to release funds.
Mitigation: the nightly pipeline must snapshot every raw file to R2 with fetch date, SHA-256 and HTTP headers. Then any published number stays traceable even if the upstream URL disappears. Show a 'last successful fetch' badge per series.

2) Login and registration gates: NASA Earthdata (NASA-SSH GMSL, GRACE mascons, JPL_RECON) and Copernicus Marine (pH OMI) need free accounts. Store tokens in the macOS Keychain locally and in GitHub Actions secrets in CI. Never ship them to the client.

3) Licence traps:
- AVISO Licence Issue 20 §3.2 bars re-hosting the raw unmodified file on a web portal or API, so offer derived monthly/annual CSVs and link to the raw file.
- Frederikse 2020's Zenodo copy is 'other-closed'; use the PO.DAAC copy.
- PSMSL has per-station conditions.
- The IAP licence is unclear, so show it only as a cross-check.
- OWID mixes licences.

4) Discontinuities and cross-producer mismatch:
- NSIDC v4 uses AMSR2 from 2025 (slightly smaller extents).
- NSIDC and OSI SAF disagree (Sep 2026: 4.81 vs 5.34 M km2), so never splice them.
- NSIDC headlines use 5-day means (4.60) while the daily CSV gives 4.574.
- AVISO is GIA-adjusted and NASA-SSH is not (about 0.3 mm/yr apart).
- CRW and Copernicus marine-heatwave baselines differ.

5) Internal inconsistencies observed:
- NASA's own pages give GMSL since 1993 as 93 mm (earth.gov, Aug 2025), 96.5 mm (Mar 2026 snippet) and 110.6 mm (sealevel.nasa.gov). Always compute from data.
- The C3S Greenland text (5,747 Gt since 1972) disagrees with its own figure CSV (-6,312 Gt by end-2025).
- The WGMS CSV uncertainty (+/-67 Gt) differs from the paper (+/-132 Gt).
- Climate Reanalyzer's legacy JSON path silently stopped in Sep 2024.

6) Coverage gaps:
- No authoritative, open, machine-readable time series exists for global marine-heatwave area or for % of reef area under bleaching stress. Compute them transparently from CRW/OISST NetCDF (Hobday 2016, code published), or cite the published statistic with its date.
- IMBIE ends Dec 2023; extensions (GRACE-FO, C3S) must be labelled separately.
- HOT ends Dec 2024 in the product file.
- Permafrost has no defensible global index; keep it site-level.
- IAP is only gridded, so the global integral must be computed.
- I could not verify the NASA-SSH, GRACE, JPL_RECON or CMEMS data values (login), the NASA AR6 tool page (JS-only) or the IMBIE Sci. Data article text (paywall redirect).

7) Cost: the daily global grids (OISST about 1.6 MB/day, CRW MHW about 1 MB/day) should be reduced in a scheduled GitHub Action to small derived CSV/JSON in R2/static hosting. The AR6 regional zips (9 GB) should be preprocessed once offline. Both keep running cost well under $20/month.

verdicts.name: Sea Ice Index, Version 4 (G02135)
verdicts.corrections:
I confirmed the data and metadata. The DOI 10.7265/a98x-0f50 resolves via DataCite to 'Sea Ice Index, Version 4', NSIDC, 2025. The Fetterer et al. (2025) citation is correct. The landing page carries the 'Basic Level of Service' notice. Every URL I listed returned 200. N_09_extent_v4.0.csv gives: 1979 7.05, 2024 4.35 (NSIDC-0051), 2025 4.75 and 2026 4.81 (NSIDC-0803), and a 1981-2010 mean of 6.4133 (n=30). In the daily CSV, the last row is 2026-10-03 at 5.771 and the 2026 minimum is 4.574 on 2026-09-12. S_09: lowest is 2023 at 16.89; 2026 is 17.32. NSIDC's analysis of 23 Sep 2026 gives 4.60 M km2 on 12 Sep, tied 10th lowest with 2008, 2010 and 2025.

CORRECTION (licence): the 'public domain' claim is not supported. https://nsidc.org/about/data-use-and-copyright makes no public-domain statement. The G02135 landing page says 'As a condition of using these data, you must cite the use of this data set.' Because citation is a condition of use, classify it as open-attribution, not public domain.

Additional findings:
(a) The v4 daily CSV draws each day's value from a 3-day centred window of source files (e.g. the 2026-10-01 row lists the 0930, 1001 and 1002 files). The newest 1-2 days use incomplete windows and will be revised, so snapshot each pull.
(b) The daily CSV header still names nsidc-0081/0051 as sources even though the rows come from NSIDC-0803 (AMSR2). Use the per-row source_dataset/Source Data column, not the header.
(c) Status nuance: NSIDC posted 'Sea Ice Today services reduced' (15 Oct 2025) and then 'Sea Ice Today returns' (19 Aug 2026). That supports, rather than contradicts, the 'at risk' label.

verdicts.name: AVISO+ Global Mean Sea Level (MSL indicators, reference-mission merged series)
verdicts.corrections:
I read the licence PDF myself: AVISO License Agreement Issue 20, effective 10 Aug 2026, Last-Modified 11 Aug 2026. Its preamble says it is CC-BY-like but explicitly NOT CC BY 4.0. §2.1 allows commercial use. §3.1 requires attribution, a link to the licence and a note of modifications. §3.2 bars sharing the original, unmodified product through a web portal, public API or cloud platform without written CNES authorisation, but does not restrict Adapted Material. Annex A puts only FES tide currents and POLYMER ocean-colour products under non-commercial terms, so the MSL indicators are fully licensed. The readme's credit wording is confirmed. The TXT has 1,236 rows from 1993.011795 to 2026.621151. Annual means: 1993 = 7.25 mm (n=37), 2025 = 111.99 mm (n=37), 2026 partial = 115.6 mm (n=23). The OLS slope is 3.414 mm/yr.

CORRECTIONS:
(1) The product page says 3.6 mm/yr (+/-0.3, 90% CI) 'from 1993', not 'since 1999'. It also gives acceleration of 0.8 +/-0.4 mm/yr/decade and about 11 cm since Feb 1993.
(2) AVISO's published rate (3.6) differs from our OLS slope on the TXT (3.41). The NetCDF carries separate variables named 'TPA_correction' and 'amr_correction', so the plain TXT column may not include the TOPEX-A and Jason-3 radiometer drift corrections that AVISO uses for its headline rate. Resolve this before publishing a rate, or label the number as 'OLS on AVISO file, computed by Environment Dashboard'.
(3) The 'third column' is the uncertainty envelope in metres: about 5.1 mm in 1993, about 1.6 mm mid-record and about 2.7 mm in 2025. The NetCDF variable is 'uncertainty_envelop'.
(4) The research describes the file's missions as TOPEX/Poseidon, Jason-1/2/3 and Sentinel-6MF. The readme lists only TOPEX/Poseidon and Jason-1/2/3; Sentinel-6 MF ('S6A') appears in the NetCDF long_name. The classification stays open-attribution, with the §3.2 restriction on raw re-hosting.

verification.headline_number_checks:
1) Arctic Sept 2026, 4.81 M km2 and -25% vs 1981-2010: CONFIRMED.
- N_09_extent_v4.0.csv: 2026 = 4.81 (NSIDC-0803).
- 1981-2010 mean = 6.4133 (n=30), so (4.81-6.4133)/6.4133 = -25.0%.
- Daily minimum 4.574 on 2026-09-12; NSIDC's 5-day figure is 4.60, tied 10th lowest (analysis of 23 Sep 2026).
- Keep the AMSR2 footnote: the -25% compares an AMSR2 year against an SSM/I-era climatology.

2) GMSL, +104.8 mm (2025 vs 1993) and 3.41 mm/yr: ARITHMETIC CONFIRMED, RATE NEEDS CORRECTION.
- My recomputation: 1993 mean 7.245 mm (n=37), 2025 mean 111.994 mm (n=37), difference 104.75 mm. OLS over 1,236 rows = 3.414 mm/yr.
- AVISO's own page says 3.6 mm/yr (+/-0.3, 90% CI) 'from 1993' and about 11 cm since Feb 1993.
- The NetCDF has separate TPA_correction and amr_correction variables, so the TXT column may lack the drift corrections behind AVISO's headline rate.
- Do not publish '3.4 mm/yr' as AVISO's rate. Either quote AVISO's 3.6 +/- 0.3 with its page and date, or label 3.41 as our own OLS on the TXT and explain the difference. The '10.5 cm' figure is fine.

3) Ocean heat, 'gained ~22 ZJ in 2025, a new record high': WORDING CORRECTED.
- Values confirmed: 32.533 - 30.316 = 2.217 x10^22 J = 22.2 ZJ, and 2025 is the record-high LEVEL.
- But 22.2 ZJ is NOT a record annual gain in this file. 2017 (+27.9 ZJ), 2006 (+24.7), 2013 (+24.6) and 2015 (+22.9) were all larger.
- Restate as: 'Ocean heat content (0-2000 m) reached a record high in 2025, about 22 ZJ more than in 2024.'
- The 0-700 m change since 1955 (22.845 - (-3.201) = 26.05 x10^22 J, about 260 ZJ) is confirmed.
- The IAP cross-check paper is Pan et al. 2026, not Cheng et al.

4) HOT pH 8.1075 to 8.0409, about +17% [H+]: CONFIRMED.
- 1989 = 8.10748 (n=10), 2024 = 8.04087 (n=7); 10^0.0666 = 1.166.
- The result is base-year sensitive (1990 = 8.1186 would give about +20%).
- An OLS fit over all 346 samples gives -0.0194 pH/decade and +16.9% [H+] over 35 years, so prefer the trend-based statement.
- EEA's 8.11 (1985) to 8.04 (2024) global figure is confirmed (published 25 Aug 2026).

5) IMBIE totals: CONFIRMED.
- Greenland -6196.15 +/- 467.35 Gt and -17.21 +/- 1.30 mm, cumulated from Jul 1971.
- Antarctica -4779.47 +/- 513.03 Gt and -13.28 +/- 1.43 mm, from Jan 1979.
- Sum 30.49 mm; the quadrature uncertainty is about +/-1.9 mm (state it).
- The mm files are signed negative, so flip the sign for 'added to sea level'.

6) WGMS glaciers: CONFIRMED.
- 2025 = -408.101 Gt (sigma 67.2), 1.126 mm SLE.
- Cumulative -9583.1 Gt (sigma 617.6), 26.436 +/- 1.704 mm (1976-2025).

7) CRW 84.4% of reef area (1 Jan 2023 to 30 Sep 2025), 68.2% for 2014-17, at least 83 countries/territories: CONFIRMED on the report page (last updated 2 Jun 2026).

8) NH snow June 2026: CONFIRMED.
- 6.227 M km2 vs a 1991-2020 June mean of 8.1337 M km2, which is -23.4%.

9) NYC Battery: CONFIRMED.
- PSMSL 2021-25 mean 7215.4 vs 1900-04 mean 6818.8 mm, a difference of 396.6 mm.
- NOAA trend 2.95 +/- 0.09 mm/yr (1856-2025).

10) AR6 2100 likely ranges 0.28-0.55 m (SSP1-1.9) and 0.63-1.01 m (SSP5-8.5), relative to 1995-2014: CONFIRMED verbatim from the SPM PDF, B.5.3.
verification.missing_sources:
1) Global Carbon Budget 2025, ocean CO2 sink.
- What it adds: the key 'cause' link. The ocean absorbs about a quarter of CO2 emissions, which drives acidification.
- Data: https://doi.org/10.18160/gcp-2025 (ICOS Carbon Portal, https://www.icos-cp.eu/GCP/2025). The 'Global Budget 2025 v1.0' xlsx includes the ocean sink.
- Licence: data use is 'conditional on citing the original data sources' (open-attribution).
- Paper: Friedlingstein et al. 2026, ESSD 18, 3211-3288, doi:10.5194/essd-18-3211-2026 (CC BY 4.0).

2) Copernicus Marine OMI 'Global Ocean Yearly CO2 Sink' (GLOBAL_OMI_HEALTH_carbon_co2_flux_integrated).
- doi:10.48670/moi-00223, covering 1985-2024. It can be downloaded anonymously via the public STAC/S3, like the pH OMI.
- Licence: Copernicus Marine licence (open-attribution).
- Related OMIs: GLOBAL_OMI_HEALTH_carbon_ph_trend (doi:10.48670/moi-00277) for a pH-trend map, and GLOBAL_OMI_TEMPSAL_sst_area_averaged_anomalies (doi:10.48670/moi-00242, 1982-2024).

3) SOCAT v2026 (Surface Ocean CO2 Atlas), https://socat.info.
- Released 16 Jun 2026, with 44 million fCO2 observations from 1957 to 2025. This is the observational basis of the ocean-sink and pH reconstructions.
- Licence: the site states CC BY 4.0. Archived at NCEI (e.g. SOCATv2023 doi:10.25921/r7xa-bt92).

4) Met Office HadSST.4.2.0.0, the long SST record (1850-2025). OISST only starts in 1981.
- Global annual CSV: https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/hadobs/hadsst4/data/data/HadSST.4.2.0.0_annual_GLOBE.csv (2025 anomaly 0.839 C, with full uncertainty columns).
- Licence: OGL v3, linked from the download page (open-attribution).
- NOAA ERSSTv5 (public domain) is the US alternative.

5) Argo GDAC, doi:10.17882/42182 (SEANOE snapshot dated 2026-09-08).
- Licence: CC BY 4.0, verified in the SEANOE metadata.
- What it adds: the in-situ backbone of every 0-2000 m OHC estimate, needed for the 'how do we know' drilldown.

6) GCOS Earth Heat Inventory: von Schuckmann et al. 2023, 'Heat stored in the Earth system 1960-2020: where does the energy go?', ESSD 15, 1675, doi:10.5194/essd-15-1675-2023.
- Licence: the paper is CC BY 4.0.
- What it adds: about 89-91% of the excess heat goes into the ocean, the central causal fact for the ocean section.
- I could not resolve the data DOI 10.26050/WDCC/GCOS_EHI_1960-2020, so verify the data licence before use.

7) Arctic sea-ice VOLUME. Extent alone hides thinning.
- PIOMAS (UW Polar Science Center): https://psc.apl.uw.edu/research/projects/arctic-sea-ice-volume-anomaly/data/. The monthly TXT resolves, but there is no licence statement (unclear), so link out only.
- Open alternative: AWI CryoSat-2/SMOS merged thickness via meereisportal.de / ESA CCI. CC BY 4.0 is expected but I did not verify it.

8) AMOC.
- Copernicus Marine OMI GLOBAL_OMI_NATLANTIC_amoc_max26N_timeseries (doi:10.48670/moi-00232; reanalysis, 1993-2023; Copernicus Marine licence).
- The RAPID-MOCHA 26N observations (rapid.ac.uk / BODC) are the observational record, but I did not verify their licence. Important for the 'consequences' story; label it carefully.

9) Ocean deoxygenation: IAP dissolved-oxygen product.
- The /ftp/cheng/ listing has 'IAP_DO_data_19602025_July2026/'.
- Licence unclear, like other IAP data; link out only.

10) UHSLC Fast Delivery tide-gauge data (https://uhslc.soest.hawaii.edu/data/).
- More current than PSMSL RLR for recent months. Licence not verified.

11) NOAA 2022 Sea Level Rise Technical Report (Sweet et al.) and NOAA high-tide-flooding outlooks (CO-OPS).
- US-government public domain. They give US local projections and nuisance-flood consequences next to AR6.
- CO-OPS pages are mid-migration, so snapshot them.

12) Greenland surface melt / daily surface mass balance: DMI/GEUS Polar Portal (polarportal.dk).
- Fills the gap between the 2023 end of IMBIE and the GRACE-FO latency.
- No licence text found (unclear); link out only.
